p: Devin's cleanup shipped a bug. A Copilot suggestion had swapped a calendar helper for plain day math, so discharge windows that crossed the November clock change ended a day early.
Fourteen hospital tickets came in before Priya rolled it back.
Renata had approved it after reading three files, because Devin was senior and it was Friday. Priya told her she'd seen the times on Friday too, and gone home.
The incident writeup had no names in it, and a line from each of them owning their part.
Renata asked about the hour that happens twice. Devin brushed her off, she asked again, and he added the test.
On Halloween night Raj set every clock in the house back by hand.
Joyce Cho. The CTO. The board meets on the twelfth, and she wants something to show it.
Anders Lindqvist. Infra on contract. His rules live in his head.
Devin Marsh. Engineer. He's reading his own pull requests now.
Renata Vega. Junior engineer. She writes everything down.
Tomasz Nowak. Leads Kraków. His team took the date bug personally.
Ken Ito. Security lead. His scanner reads every pull request.

The clocks had gone back on Sunday and her body hadn't, so on Monday she was up an hour before she needed to be. Priya spent it at the kitchen table with her old runbook, the one with "ask Anders" written in the margins in her own handwriting, and counted. Twenty three.

Then she started a second list: the rules at Halcyon that weren't written down anywhere. A discharge window is calendar days, in the hospital's own time zone. Never build SQL by gluing strings together. Log request IDs, never request bodies. Run date tests in a time zone that changes its clocks. She stopped at eleven. Every one of them lived in somebody's head, and one had lived in the name of a helper function until a cleanup called it unused and deleted it.
At 6:50 a message came in from Tomasz in Kraków. Eight hours again. Our week as neighbors is over.

An email from Joyce Cho. Subject: The 12th. Elena's board is a week from Thursday. She'll ask one question about Copilot: what did we change so last week can't happen again. I'd like the answer to be something we can open and read. Joyce
Asha's cards came at 7:30, five photos, purple felt tip. Across the top card: Week five. House rules. Every unit I ever worked had a binder of them. The good ones were thin.
Asha's first card said: The house rules lived at the nurses' station, not in the charge nurse's head. If only one person knows a rule, the unit doesn't have it.
The second card: The ICU's rules aren't the ER's rules. Don't make the ER read the ICU's binder.
The third card: A protocol tells you what to look for. It can't sign the chart for you.
The fourth card: We had order sets for the things we did every night. Same steps for every nurse, so nobody was inventing it at three in the morning.
The last card: Don't describe a good chart to a new nurse. Show them three.

At nine she put the list on the screen in the small conference room. Joyce had coffee. Devin had his laptop closed in front of him, which was new. Ken stood by the door. He had somewhere to be and had come anyway.
These are good. Where do they live, so Copilot actually reads them? I'm not paying for a tool that has to be told the same thing ninety times a day.
And wherever they live, I want to be able to show Nora who changed them, and when.

She creates the Copilot instructions file in Lumen's .github folder on a branch and opens a pull request, so the rules get reviewed like code. Ken likes that the history will show every change and who made it. Joyce asks how they'll know Copilot read it. When Chat uses it, the file shows up in the answer's references.
By Monday afternoon the file existed, and it was empty.

Joyce sent her a link to an old wiki page called Things Lumen Doesn't Tell You. It ran to eleven screens: the history of every product decision, a long section on why the scheduler retries, a joke about a holiday party, and, halfway down, the date rule, in the middle of a paragraph.

I wrote that at two in the morning in 2023, the night of our first clock change bug. I wrote addCalendarDays the same night. She said it lightly, and she didn't look at Priya while she said it. Nobody's opened the page since. I checked.
Can we paste it in? All of it's still true.

It takes an hour to get eleven screens down to one page. Short statements under plain headings: what Lumen does, the languages and frameworks, the commands to build and test, and the rules, one line each. The date rule gets two lines and a small example of what to do and what not to. Joyce reads it twice. That's what I meant to write in 2023.
Tuesday morning the file was open on her second monitor.

Her draft of copilot instructions dot M D, the file in the dot github folder. It says Lumen does discharge forecasting for hospitals, with TypeScript services, PostgreSQL, and Terraform in the infra folder, and to run npm ci, then npm test, with date tests set to Denver time. Then three rules: a discharge window is calendar days in the hospital's time zone, so use the add calendar days helper and never multiply days by a fixed day length; build SQL with parameters, never by joining strings; and log request IDs, never request bodies.

Anders read it over her shoulder at ten, coffee in hand. Fine. Now where do mine go? Always plan before apply. Never the flag that skips the yes or no question. The staging database has prevent_destroy on it and it stays that way.
He tapped the screen. Not in there, though. Forty people writing TypeScript don't need my state files in every answer they get.
He'd written the first of those rules himself, two weeks ago, under his own name.

The file is six lines under a short front matter block, with an applyTo line that points it at every Terraform file under infra. Copilot uses it, along with the repository wide file, whenever the file in play matches that pattern, and nowhere else. Anders opens the staging module, asks Copilot Chat what it does, and reads the answer while his coffee goes cold. It knows about prevent_destroy now. That's more than the last contractor knew. He's the last contractor. He lets her laugh at that.
Wednesday morning Devin waved her over to his desk.
The yellow page that said Careful was taped to the bottom of his monitor, turned so it faced him and not the room.
The file doesn't work. Watch. In a scratch file he typed const end new Date(start.getTime() and stopped. Gray text appeared after the cursor: days 86400000.
It's right there in the rules. Never multiply by 86400000. And it suggests it anyway.

She has him ask Copilot Chat to finish the same line. The answer uses addCalendarDays in the hospital's time zone, and under References is Lumen's instructions file. So the gray text never saw it. Not in VS Code. The file shapes chat, agents, and reviews, not suggestions as you type. That part's still yours. Devin deletes the gray text and types the helper name himself.
Wednesday afternoon Renata and Devin brought her the part of the file meant for Copilot code review. They'd written it together. Priya noticed that, and didn't mention it.
It started from Friday's review rule, the one with whoever wrote it in bold, and tried to teach Copilot the same habits.

Their review section, five lines. Flag day math that multiplies by a fixed day length and suggest the add calendar days helper in the hospital's zone, and flag SQL built by joining strings and suggest a parameterized query. Then block merging until every Copilot comment is resolved, review against the standards at a link to the team wiki, and be thorough and don't miss anything.
Is this how you do it? I wasn't sure which of these it can actually do.

They keep the first two lines and add a short right and wrong code example under each. The wiki line goes, because Copilot code review doesn't follow outside links. "Be thorough" goes, because it doesn't tell Copilot anything. Merge blocking moves where it belongs, to a branch ruleset that requires a human approval and resolved comments. Renata writes the reason for each cut in her notebook, one per line.
Thursday at seven Tomasz had his camera on. He had something to show her.
After last week, my team wrote date tests for every service. I read them all. Seven engineers, seven prompts, seven kinds of test. One of them only tested October. Can we have one way to ask?
Behind him his engineers had their editors open, and two of them were already typing.

Tomasz's best engineer writes date-tests.prompt.md: a one line description in the front matter, then the steps. State the rule first, list the edges, take expected values from the rule, never from current output. It links to the instructions file instead of copying it. In VS Code anyone types a slash and date-tests in chat and gets the same start. Tomasz asks the right question. And on GitHub? Prompt files are for the IDE. VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains. The cloud agent reads the instructions files instead.

At 10:14 Ken's scanner flagged a pull request. It read every pull request at Halcyon for secrets, patient identifiers, and a list of bad patterns Ken had been adding to for years, and it was rarely wrong. This one was Renata's.

She'd been writing a second prompt file, for test fixtures. Asked once with no examples, Copilot had given her fixtures in the wrong shape: one date field instead of three, times with no zones. So she'd pasted five rows from the staging database into the prompt as examples. Staging was seeded from scrubbed data, mostly. Two of the rows still had real looking dates of birth.
Renata reached Priya's desk a minute before Ken's message did.
I'm closing it. I only wanted it to see the format. Am I in trouble?

You're not in trouble. The scanner did its job, and so did you, coming here. They write three fixtures by hand, all invented: an admission at 11:58 PM, one at the first 1:30 on a clock change night, one at noon, each with three date fields and a time zone. Under them, one line: vary the times and zones, keep the shape. Copilot's next twenty fixtures match. Ken approves the new pull request with one word. Better.
At the Thursday sync Renata put her hand halfway up, then down, then up again.
Priya saw it the first time and stopped talking. Renata.

This is probably basic. I asked Chat what's wrong with this window, and it told me about the export query. Then Devin asked the same question on his laptop and got the right answer. Why would it answer us differently?
Devin turned his laptop around: one file open, the window function selected. Renata had nine tabs open. Three of them were the old export.

Renata closes six tabs, selects calculateWindow, and asks what's wrong with calculateWindow. The answer is about calculateWindow. So 'this' was doing a lot of work. Half the room laughs, kindly, and two people quietly close tabs of their own.
Friday morning Devin had a chat open with a single prompt in it.

A message from Devin's prompt. Refactor the nightly census job to use parameterized queries the way we fixed the export, add tests for every edge case, update the docs, make it faster, and fix anything else you see.
The answer was six hundred lines across eleven files. Devin scrolled to the bottom and back up.
I can't review this. I mean I can. Not carefully.

He starts over. First prompt: rewrite the census query with parameters, nothing else. He reads it, runs the tests, commits. Then tests for the census job, naming the edges. Then the docs. By noon it's three small commits instead of one big one, each something a reviewer can actually read. Performance waits for next week, with a ticket.

At one Priya asked Copilot Chat to draft her summary for Joyce: what the house rules were, where they lived, and how they worked. She'd used the same chat thread all week, since seven on Monday morning.
The draft was mostly right. It also described the eleven rules the way she'd first sketched them on Monday, before anyone had read them, three of which the team had cut by Tuesday.
Her own chat history, she realized, had more of Monday in it than Friday.

The new thread starts with the instructions files, the prompt files, and one line about Joyce's question. The summary comes back with this week's rules and none of Monday's. She doesn't delete the old thread. She just stops carrying it.
At three she opened the pull request with the house rules in it: the repository wide file, Anders's Terraform file, the review section, and two prompt files. Then she sat looking at the reviewer box.
The runbook was open beside her keyboard. All week she'd been crossing out margins as the rules went into files. Nine were gone, the Terraform ones last.
For years the reviewer on nearly everything she wrote had been Anders. She typed his name.

He came over instead of commenting, which he never did. He looked at the runbook, at his own name with a line through it in her pen, a second longer than he needed to. Before I approve this. How do you know Copilot follows any of it?

They push a scratch commit to the same branch: the old line, days 86400000, and a query glued together from strings. Copilot code review reads instructions from the pull request's own branch, so the new rules are live for this review before anything merges. It flags the day math and suggests addCalendarDays. It misses the SQL. Anders rewrites that rule with a short example, they run it again, and it catches both. They drop the scratch commit. He approves at 4:40 with one comment. Read it anyway.
The house rules merged on Friday afternoon, tested on a pull request with the old bug planted in it on purpose. Anders's approval was the last thing on the page.
Joyce answered her summary at 6:10 with one line. Can I delete the wiki page now?
Priya thought about it longer than the question needed. Leave it. Somebody wrote it at two in the morning.
Ken's last message of the week came at 6:20. The scanner sees pull requests. It never saw what went to Copilot before one was opened. Monday I want to talk about staging.
On the way out Renata stopped her to ask if she could own the fixtures prompt. Priya said yes before she'd finished asking.
It had been a quieter week than the last one, and she'd needed that. She had written more than she'd decided, and for once that felt like the job.
Sunday was dinner in Aurora. Asha's shoes were already by the door, and the kitchen smelled like her grandmother's dal. There was an argument going.
She never measured. She did it by hand.
She measured. With the steel cup. Her father took it down from the shelf, a small dented cup with the lip worn smooth. This one. Two of these of dal. Half of this of jaggery.
Half? Raj. It was never half.

They'd been having this argument, Priya realized, for as long as she could remember. Nobody had written it down, because their mother had been in the kitchen, and then Raj had, and it had never seemed necessary.
Asha's bag on the counter had index cards in it. It always did. Priya took a blank one, and Asha handed her the purple felt tip without being asked.

She wrote while they cooked. Two steel cups of toor dal. Jaggery: half a cup, says Raj. More, says Asha. Tamarind about the size of a thumb. Mustard seeds until they pop. When the card was full she held it up.
Her father took the felt tip and added one line at the bottom, in the square capitals he'd used on job tickets for thirty one years. ASK ASHA.
Asha looked at it for a moment. Then she took the pen back and wrote underneath, smaller. Ask Raj.
Most of the margins in her runbook had been rules, and rules belonged in a file. A few had been questions only a person could answer. Those, she decided, could stay.
Her father put the card on the refrigerator under a magnet from a hardware store that had closed in 1998, and they ate.
